answer:
**Residual vector quantization improves an approximation in stages.** An encoder first maps audio into continuous latent vectors. The first codebook chooses a nearby vector. The next codebook approximates the error that remains, and later codebooks continue refining that residual. The decoder receives the sum of the chosen vectors. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.13438)

A one-dimensional illustration makes the idea concrete. Suppose the latent value is 2.7. The first stage chooses 2.0, leaving 0.7. The second chooses 0.5, leaving 0.2. The third chooses 0.2, reconstructing 2.7. Real codebooks contain multidimensional vectors, and the learned choices need not resemble these simple decimal increments.

Only codebook indices need to be transmitted or modeled. If there are eight codebooks, 1024 entries per codebook, and 50 latent frames per second, the raw index rate is $8\times\log_2(1024)\times50=4000$ bits/s, before entropy coding and other overhead. This is an illustrative configuration, not a universal codec specification.

More stages generally permit better reconstruction at greater bitrate and modeling cost. Dropping later stages supports variable quality only when the system is trained and designed for it. Earlier and later codebooks are coarse-to-fine in residual reconstruction, but that does not guarantee a clean semantic division such as words in one stage and speaker identity in another.

**Technical details and references.**

An audio encoder produces continuous latent vectors. The first codebook approximates a vector; each subsequent codebook quantizes the residual left by previous stages. The decoder reconstructs audio from the sum of selected code vectors. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.13438)

$$r_0=z,\quad q_k=\arg\min_{e\in C_k}\|r_{k-1}-e\|^2,\quad r_k=r_{k-1}-q_k,\quad \hat z=\sum_kq_k.$$

The discrete indices form several synchronized token streams. More codebooks increase bitrate and usually fidelity; dropping later stages offers a rate/quality tradeoff when training supports it. Token rate, codebook size, and number of stages determine raw bitrate before entropy coding. Coarse-to-fine residual structure is not guaranteed to map cleanly to human concepts such as words versus timbre.
